name: Smart home and home automation
definition: A house whose lighting, doors, appliances and services are run automatically by machines responding to its occupants.

first_pass.what: Westinghouse engineer Jim Sutherland's ECHO IV home computer was operational in his house, running household tasks with keypads and terminals around the home.

first_pass_note: Mass adoption (X10 1975, Amazon Echo 2014) not verified.

name: Automatic sensor door
definition: A door that opens by itself when a sensor detects a person approaching.

first_pass.what: Dee Horton and Lew Hewitt founded Horton Automatics and put the first commercial automatic sliding door on the market. It was mat-actuated; they invented it in 1954. An earlier 1931 Stanley optical door is unconfirmed.

first_pass_note: The 1931 Stanley optical door and 1980 infrared sensor were not independently confirmed.

name: Fully automated city
definition: A city or settlement whose services and infrastructure are run entirely by machines and a central computer.
first_pass_note: No fully automated city exists; PlanIT Valley and Songdo are planned or smart-city projects, so no milestone.

name: Automated environmental monitoring
definition: Networks of automatic sensors and computers that record weather, water or air and forecast or control them.

first_pass.what: Charney, Fjørtoft and von Neumann ran the first computer weather forecast on ENIAC, published in 1950. The forecast itself may date to 1949.

The Joint Numerical Weather Prediction Unit in Suitland, Maryland, began operational numerical forecasting in May 1955 using a three-level model. The Swedish BESK computer ran routine forecasts from December 1954.

first_pass_note: Milestones cover numerical weather prediction; automatic weather stations were not searched.

name: Teaching machine and computer-assisted instruction
definition: A machine or computer that presents lessons, tests students and grades their answers automatically.

first_pass.what: Sidney Pressey at Ohio State University created a mechanical teaching machine that tested students with multiple-choice questions. Skinner's machine followed in 1954, and PLATO began at the University of Illinois around 1960.

first_pass_note: Practical use and mass adoption not given; PLATO date conflicts across sources.

name: Computerized medical records and diagnosis
definition: Computers that store patient records and diagnose disease or choose treatment from symptoms and test results.

first_pass.what: MYCIN, a rule-based expert system for diagnosing bacterial infections and recommending antibiotics, developed at Stanford (Shortliffe's doctoral work); never used clinically

first_pass_note: MYCIN is a demonstration only, never clinically deployed; no practical-use or mass-adoption milestone confirmed

name: Computer psychological analysis and therapy
definition: A computer that assesses personality or mental state and conducts psychotherapy with a patient.

first_pass.what: Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT published ELIZA (DOCTOR script), a program simulating a Rogerian psychotherapist; a pattern-matching analogue, not a true assessment or therapy system

first_pass_note: ELIZA is a shallow pattern-matching analogue; no true computer assessment and therapy confirmed

name: Lie detector
definition: A device that detects deception by measuring physiological signals such as pulse, breathing and skin conductance.

first_pass.what: John Larson, a Berkeley police officer, built the first operational polygraph (cardio-pneumo-psychogram) at Chief August Vollmer's request
Larson used the polygraph in a Berkeley police investigation of dormitory thefts, questioning the residents

first_pass_note: mass_adoption not researched (Keeler popularised the polygraph in the US)

name: Electroencephalography and brain-wave analysis
definition: Recording the brain's electrical activity through electrodes to analyse mental states or diagnose disorders.

first_pass.what: Hans Berger made the first human EEG recording in Jena in 1924 (date of 6 July reported by some sources); he published it in 1929

first_pass_note: practical clinical use and mass adoption not researched

name: Mind-reading machine
definition: A machine that reads a person's specific thoughts, memories or images directly from their brain.

first_pass.what: Nishimoto, Gallant et al. (UC Berkeley) reconstructed approximate movie clips a subject had watched from fMRI brain activity (Current Biology, Sept 2011); a partial, limited fit to the definition

first_pass_note: only coarse visual reconstruction from fMRI; specific thoughts and memories not read, so a partial match
doubt: 2011 fMRI movie reconstruction is a stretch for 'mind-reading'; check whether the concept has a real milestone at all and whether earlier decoding of thoughts fits.

name: Thought-to-text and thought display
definition: A machine that writes down a person's thoughts as text, or shows their mental images or dreams on a screen.

first_pass.what: Willett et al. (Stanford, BrainGate) decoded imagined handwriting from motor cortex of a paralysed man into on-screen text at about 90 characters/min (Nature, May 2021)

first_pass_note: imagined handwriting and speech decoding in clinical trials only; no routine use

name: Brain-computer interface
definition: A link from the brain's electrical signals to a machine, so that a person controls devices by thought alone.

first_pass.what: Jacques Vidal at UCLA showed a noninvasive EEG visual-evoked-potential interface letting a user move a cursor through a maze, following his 1973 paper proposing the brain-computer interface

first_pass_note: later invasive BCIs and practical use not researched

name: Neural implant and cyborg augmentation
definition: An electronic device implanted in or joined to the human body or brain to restore or extend senses, memory or ability.

first_pass.what: William House and John Doyle in Los Angeles implanted gold-insulated electrodes in the cochleas of two deaf patients
The FDA approved marketing of the 3M/House single-channel cochlear implant for adults in the US

first_pass_note: cochlear implant used as the example; mass adoption not researched

name: Human brain or mind in a machine body
definition: A living human brain, or a transferred human mind, housed in and controlling a robot or machine body.

name: Mind uploading
definition: Copying or transferring a human mind into a computer, where it continues to think.
